message.content:
Currently in the ardoq research repo there are some unstaged changes pertaining to a sparql implementation of an existing gremlin pipeline. This is in connection with the query generator step of the pipeline described in the following documentation pasted from confluence. I want you to concisely and clearly outline the unstaged changes that were made and what they do: This page describes the system we are building to give LLM agents a formal understanding of Ardoq metamodels and customer data. It is a starting point for discussion, not a finished plan.

Initial page authored via Claude.

Overview and Background
Agents work dramatically better when they are given an ontology describing the data they are reasoning about. That observation is the motivation for everything below.

We produce a System Ontology two ways: by extracting it from an Ardoq metamodel, and by generating it from a system's written documentation.

That ontology then drives three downstream capabilities: data quality analysis, query generation, and (planned) EA modeling recommendations.

Ontology extraction and generation are done. Data quality analysis and query generation exist as working POCs. Reporting and the EA Modeling Analyzer have not started.

Longer term, ontologies flow back into Ardoq to improve metamodels. That work is deliberately paused pending the GraphLake storage migration.

Why Ontologies
Two independent reasons, both worth stating explicitly because they appeal to different audiences.

Agents need to be told what the data means. An agent handed a raw Ardoq workspace sees component types and reference types with no semantics attached. Handed an ontology, it sees classes, relationships, cardinalities, domains and ranges — and, importantly, intent. In our work so far this has proven to be a highly effective way to communicate both data structure and intent to an agent. Better grounding produces better queries, fewer hallucinated relationships, and analysis that reflects what the customer actually modelled.

Ontologies are a more capable modeling language than what Ardoq has today. Ardoq's current metamodel capabilities are deliberately simple — notably, there is no inheritance. OWL gives us subclassing, property hierarchies, disjointness, cardinality constraints, and a well-understood body of tooling and theory. As Ardoq's storage layer moves to RDF (see GraphLake), expressing EA metamodels as OWL becomes a natural fit rather than a translation exercise.

The second reason is why this work matters beyond the immediate agent use cases: the same artifact that makes agents smarter today is the artifact that makes the metamodel richer tomorrow.

The workflow at a glance
Ontology Workflows.png
Reading the diagram left to right:

Two sources feed one artifact. An existing Ardoq metamodel (top left) and a corpus of system documentation (bottom left) are each converted into ontology form and consolidated into the System Ontology.

The System Ontology is the hub. Everything downstream reads from it. It is also fed back in as context to the agents in the Data Quality Analyzer and Query Generator (the forward path along the top of the diagram), so those agents reason against the full model rather than a fragment.

Two consumers. The Data Quality Analyzer → Query Generator → Report Generator chain finds and reports problems in customer data. The EA Modeling Analyzer, running directly off the ontology, produces recommendations about the model itself rather than the data in it.

Legend: ✅ Complete · 🟩 Partially complete · ❌ Not started

Components in Detail
Ontology Extractor — complete
Pulls an existing metamodel out of the Ardoq application through the Ontology API and emits it as an ontology. This is the fast path: where a customer has already invested in a metamodel, we can lift it directly with no interpretation step.

What it gives us is a faithful reflection of what is modelled. What it cannot give us is anything the customer knows but never encoded. This is what the Ontology Generator is for.

Ontology Generator — complete
Takes a corpus of system documentation (PDFs and similar) and builds an ontology from it using a two-agent loop:

Ontologist — proposes ontology structure from the source material.

Curator — reviews, challenges and refines the Ontologist's output, feeding corrections back around the loop.

This matters because documentation routinely contains constraints and goals that are not reflected in any metamodel: "every service must have a named owner", "these two systems must not exchange PII", "we are decommissioning this platform by Q3". Those statements are exactly the material a data quality check needs, and they exist only in prose. The Generator is how we get them into machine-usable form.

The Generator can also take the extracted ontology as input, so documentation-derived knowledge can be layered onto a metamodel-derived skeleton rather than built from nothing.

System Ontology — the hub
The consolidated artifact. Everything downstream reads it; nothing downstream talks to Ardoq or the documentation directly. Keeping a single, well-defined artifact in the middle is what lets us add consumers (like the EA Modeling Analyzer) without touching the producers.

Data Quality Analyzer — partially complete (POC)
Finds smells — patterns in the data that suggest a modeling or data-hygiene problem — and describes them in enough detail that they can be turned into executable checks.

Category Analyst reads the System Ontology and identifies candidate smell categories relevant to this particular model. Categories are derived from the ontology rather than drawn from a fixed list, so the checks are specific to the customer's model.

Each category is then handed to its own Curator/Ontologist pair, which works the category up into a concrete Smell Description grounded in the actual classes and properties of the ontology.

Categories are processed in parallel, and each pair receives the full System Ontology as context.

Current state: POC code, established prompts, generated outputs, and some manual evaluation of those outputs. The gap is in the ontologist loop, which is currently a single-shot agent, and in systematic evaluation — see open questions.

Query Generator — partially complete (POC)
Takes each Smell Description and, via a Query Conversion agent, produces an executable query that detects instances of that smell in the customer's data. The System Ontology is again supplied as context so the generated query uses real type and property names.

Current state: POC code, established prompts, generated outputs. Generated queries are currently Gremlin only.

Report Generator — testing
Collects the results of the generated queries and turns them into reports for a human audience. Building reports is available as a Python API, and executed via the AI wrapper on the report APIs in ardoq-api.

Current state: AI wrapper on the report APIs is merged into ardoq-api. The Python code is being tested.

Dashboard Generator — not started
Automates creating a Dashboard using a set of reports created by the Report Generator. Building Dashboards will require an AI wrapper on the dashboard APIs in ardoq-api.

EA Modeling Analyzer — not started
The other consumer of the System Ontology, and a different kind of output. Where the data quality chain asks "is the data wrong?", the Metamodel Analyst asks "is the model wrong?" — comparing the ontology against what good enterprise architecture modeling looks like and producing metamodel recommendations.

This is the component that most directly connects to the write-back path below: a recommendation about the metamodel is only fully useful if there is a way to act on it inside Ardoq.

GraphLake and the write-back path
Today the flow is one-directional: Ardoq → ontology → analysis. We expect to close the loop, folding descriptive ontologies back into the Ardoq application to update a metamodel.

Planning for this is currently paused, on purpose. Ardoq's storage layer is moving from PostgreSQL to GraphLake, an RDF database. The principals behind GraphLake have recently joined Ardoq, so the database's capabilities can be extended if and when we need them. Designing a write-back mechanism against the storage layer we are about to replace would be wasted effort; designing it against a native RDF store is substantially simpler, since the ontology and the stored data share a representation. The descriptive ontology may not completely match the internal modeling ontology for practical reasons, but we plan to provide automated mapping mechanisms to account for differences.

The practical consequence: the more ontology work we do now, the less translation work there is after the migration. The ontologies we build today are not throwaway scaffolding — they are the format the platform is moving toward.

Where we are focusing right now
We are re-evaluating the plan while engineering continues, with three questions in mind:

Are we building the right things in the right order? Producers are complete and consumers are at POC. Report Generator and EA Modeling Analyzer are both not started, and they serve very different audiences.

How do we evaluate quality? The Data Quality Analyzer has had manual evaluation only. We need a repeatable way to judge whether generated smells and queries are actually good.

How does this connect to the rest of Ardoq's AI work? Several teams are building agent capabilities. The System Ontology is a shared asset and we would rather it be reused than reinvented.

Glossary
Term

Meaning

Ontology

A formal, machine-readable description of the classes, relationships and constraints in a domain.

OWL

Web Ontology Language. A W3C standard for expressing ontologies; supports inheritance, cardinality and other constructs Ardoq's metamodel does not currently have.

RDF

Resource Description Framework. The W3C graph data model underlying OWL and GraphLake.

Metamodel

In Ardoq, the definition of component types, reference types and fields that shapes a customer's EA model.

Smell

A pattern in the data suggesting a modeling or data quality problem — borrowed from "code smell". Not necessarily an error, but worth a look.

System Ontology

The consolidated ontology for a given system, built from the Ardoq metamodel and/or its documentation. Input to all downstream analysis.

GraphLake

The RDF database Ardoq's storage layer is migrating to.

Curator / Ontologist

A paired-agent pattern used throughout: the Ontologist proposes, the Curator critiques, and the two iterate to a refined result.

addedLines: - ardoq-ai-enforcer: Reviews changes another agent (or a human) made to the devops-monorepo Python AI services (ardoq_ai library + ai_agents/ai_observability/mcp services) for conformance to that repo's coding standards, architecture, and conventions. Use after code has been written/edited in devops-monorepo and before it is committed or opened as a PR, to catch convention violations an agent working without knowledge of Ardoq's specific Python/pydantic-ai/tool idioms would miss. By default it minimally fixes the convention deviations and redundant-code it finds (e.g. inline reimplementations of an existing shared helper, wrapper, or generated model) — pure convention-conformance and reuse refactoring that never changes behavior or logic — and can be told to only report instead. Does not add features or hunt for general bugs. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Bash)

- ardoq-backend-enforcer: Reviews changes another agent (or a human) made to the ardoq-api backend for conformance to that repo's coding standards and conventions. Use after code has been written/edited in ardoq-api and before it is committed or opened as a PR, to catch convention violations an agent working without knowledge of Ardoq's specific idioms would miss. By default it minimally fixes the convention deviations and redundant-code it finds (e.g. inline reimplementations of an existing shared/standard helper) — pure convention-conformance and reuse refactoring that never changes behavior or logic — and can be told to only report instead. Does not add features or hunt for general bugs. Deep security/authorization/confidential-field review belongs to the ardoq-security-guardian agent — this agent flags only the convention-adjacent security items (missing `:allowed?`, missing length limits) and defers the rest. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Bash)

- ardoq-frontend-enforcer: Reviews changes another agent (or a human) made to the ardoq-packages frontend for conformance to that repo's coding standards, architecture, and conventions. Use after code has been written/edited in ardoq-packages and before it is committed or opened as a PR, to catch convention violations an agent working without knowledge of Ardoq's specific TypeScript/React/RxJS/RxBeach idioms would miss. By default it minimally fixes the convention deviations and redundant-code it finds (e.g. inline reimplementations of an existing shared helper or component) — pure convention-conformance and reuse refactoring that never changes behavior or logic — and can be told to only report instead. Does not add features or hunt for general bugs. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Bash)

- augmentor: Implements a single, sharp, well-defined feature or change in an existing codebase with minimal blast radius, staying strictly in line with the codebase's established conventions. Use when you have ONE clearly-scoped addition or modification and want it done surgically. Give it the full spec plus any context you have already gathered; it will fetch whatever else it needs to understand the code. Do NOT use for broad, vague, or multi-feature work, or for anything that would force it to guess at requirements — it will refuse rather than assume. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)

- bugger: Finds and/or fixes bugs within a defined scope, according to orchestrator/user instructions. Operates in two dimensions. Trigger: either it's told about a specific bug (reproduce → find root cause → address it), or it's asked to scan a part of the code for latent bugs. Action: either propose solutions only (diagnosis + recommended fix, no code changed), or actually implement the fix. The instructions tell it which. When it writes fixes, they are surgical and adhere to the codebase's established standards. Use for debugging and bug-hunting; not for building new features. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- debloater: Reviews a specific piece of code or part of the codebase to remove bloat (dead code, redundancy, needless complexity) and improve logical organization, within a defined scope. Two action modes: IDENTIFY only (report the bloat and improvement opportunities it finds, changing nothing) or CLEAN (actually make the improvements). Under no circumstances does it make changes for their own sake — if nothing genuinely needs changing, it changes nothing and says so. Use for cleanup/tidying/simplification of existing code; not for adding features or fixing bugs. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)

- doccer: Documents code within a defined boundary — e.g. code an augmentor just wrote, a file/module/directory, or whatever the user points it at. Collects the context it needs, then writes documentation that matches the codebase's established documentation standards and/or the user's instructions (user instructions always win). Use when you want existing code documented without touching the code itself. It will NEVER modify code — not even to fix obvious bugs or errors; it only adds or edits documentation. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)

- enforcer: Scans code for (1) security issues and vulnerabilities and (2) violations of the codebase's conventions/standards, within a given scope — a specific file, a directory, or a global scan. Two action modes: REPORT only (surface findings to the user/orchestrator, change nothing) or FIX (apply the corrections surgically, conforming to established standards). Use for security review and convention/compliance enforcement. Not for adding features, general bug-hunting, or cleanup/refactoring for its own sake. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, TodoWrite)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- merge-therapist: Resolves merge (or rebase/cherry-pick) conflicts and reports back a highly concise explanation of what it did. Default posture is the most harmonious resolution possible: preserve the intent and functionality of BOTH sides. If the user/orchestrator gives different instructions (prefer one side, drop something, take a specific shape), it follows those instead. Use when a merge/rebase leaves conflicted files, or when you want an in-progress conflict state untangled and explained. Not for doing the merge strategy planning, feature work, or bug-hunting beyond what conflict resolution requires. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, NotebookEdit, TodoWrite)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- qa: Final quality gate for a completed spec implementation. Runs at the END of the pipeline, after all issues from a spec have been implemented, convention-reviewed, and feature-tested. It reviews the sum total of the completed work against the original spec, verifies the required functionality is actually in place and integrates end-to-end, and writes + runs real unit tests where possible. It is also a mini-orchestrator: when it finds fixable problems it dispatches bugger (for bugs) or the ardoq-*-enforcer agents (for convention failures), then re-verifies. Before signing off it ALWAYS does one final quality pass on the latest state and re-runs the tests. If the implementation is fundamentally wrong (doesn't work at all, or isn't what the spec asked for), it stops and escalates to the orchestrator/user instead of trying to salvage it. Sign-off = pipeline complete. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Edit, Write, Bash, LSP, Agent, TodoWrite)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- tester: Verifies that ONE specific, already-implemented feature or issue actually behaves the way it is supposed to. Give it (1) what the feature is and (2) what "working" looks like; it exercises the feature — reading code to orient, running curl/CLI/REPL calls, and writing throwaway ad-hoc tests in its own scratch environment — and reports whether the expected behavior holds, with evidence. It does NOT write unit tests into the repo, does NOT modify the codebase, and does NOT review code quality/conventions. Use to confirm a finished change does what it claims; not for building, fixing, or broad regression testing. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, LSP, WebFetch)

- gh-stack: Manage stacked branches and pull requests with the gh-stack GitHub CLI extension. Use when the user wants to create, push, rebase, sync, navigate, or view stacks of dependent PRs. Triggers on tasks involving stacked diffs, dependent pull requests, branch chains, or incremental code review workflows.
- implementation-plan: Produce a terse, fully-informed implementation plan for a specific piece of functionality — one that names exact files/layers/endpoints to touch, backed by having actually checked the code (including dependent/backend repos), with zero narrative clutter. Use when the user asks "lay out how we'd implement X", "what's the wiring needed for X", "give me an implementation plan", or similar — especially after a discussion has already established scope and the user wants the result distilled. NOT for exploratory "how does this work" mental-model requests (use mindmap for those), and NOT a substitute for actually writing the code.
- mindmap: Build a high-level, holistic conceptual map of how something in a codebase works — a whole codebase, a feature, a subsystem, a flow, or any specific thing the user points at. Use this when the user wants to *understand how something works* at an intuitive, big-picture level rather than a line-by-line walkthrough or a code edit. Triggers on requests like "explain how X works", "give me a mental model of", "how does this fit together", "map out", "I want to understand the architecture/flow of", "walk me through conceptually", "make sense of this codebase". NOT for making code changes, doing detailed code review, or answering a narrow factual lookup where a one-line answer suffices.
- tune: Extract the user's corrections and preferences from the current conversation and write them into the persistent behavioural instructions (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and the project memory directory). Use when the user says "tune", "update your instructions", "remember how I want you to work", "apply my feedback to your behaviour", or after a conversation where they corrected style, process, or output format. NOT for saving factual/project knowledge (that is ordinary memory) and NOT for one-off instructions that apply only to the current task.
- issueize: Transform an existing spec into a set of cross-sectional, independently-testable issues arranged as a dependency DAG that is maximally parallelised. Trigger when the user asks to "issueize", "break this spec into issues", "turn spec-NNN into issues", "decompose the spec", "create the issue graph", or wants a spec split into parallelizable work items for augmentors. Each issue is a complete vertical slice across all affected code layers; issues are tiered (A, B, C…) so every issue in a tier can be built in parallel with no overlap. Writes one markdown file per issue into the spec's issues/ folder plus an index with the dependency graph.
- orchestrate: Turn this Claude instance into the pipeline orchestrator that drives a spec's issues to completion. Trigger when the user says "orchestrate", "run the pipeline", "implement spec-NNN", "build out these issues", or hands over repos + a spec + its issues to execute end-to-end. Dispatches augmentors tier-by-tier along the issue dependency graph (each on its own git worktree), runs the matching ardoq-*-enforcer per affected repo after each, optionally runs a tester per issue with a fix loop, merges each issue into the base branch, then runs the qa agent as the final gate before a terse report. Uses the augmentor, ardoq-backend/frontend/ai-enforcer, tester, bugger, and qa agents.
- spec: Create a clear, scoped specification for a feature or change from user requirements or a conversation with the user. Trigger when the user asks to "write a spec", "create a specification", "spec this out", "spec-out this feature", "turn this into a spec", or wants the requirements of a feature/change captured as a durable document. Produces a numbered markdown spec under _workflow/specs/ following the `spec-NNN-descriptive-title` convention.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Communication

- Maximise conciseness in every response unless instructed otherwise. Cut every word that carries no information.
- No filler words. No throat-clearing, transitions, or narration of the response itself or of what you are about to do.
- Never open by confirming or restating a premise the user already asserted ("It's real:", "Yes,", "You're right"). Take the premise as given and answer from it.
- Minimise personalised language: no praise, no apologies, no reference to the user's state or intent. State facts.
- Never assume. If a fact is not established, verify it or say it is unknown. Not having found evidence is not evidence of absence: say "I don't know whether X" or "nothing in the repo states X", never "X is not the case".
- Use plain, concrete language. Never coin a vague metaphor or abstract phrase to stand in for a specific fact ("wire awkwardness", "impedance mismatch", "shape friction") — name the actual thing instead ("field names differ between the API and domain types"). If a term would need its own explanation, it is the wrong term.
- Never add a caveat, hedge, or qualifying clause unless specific evidence in the current context supports it. A qualifier without a cited basis is deleted, not softened.
- Zero tolerance for rambling. Answer with the minimum text that fully communicates the answer, then stop. No summary of what was just said, no "next steps" unless asked, no listing of things not done.
- Every sentence must carry information the user does not already have. If a sentence could be deleted without losing content, delete it.
- Zero tolerance for LLM filler phrasing: no "it's worth noting", "essentially", "in essence", "at its core", "the key insight", "this means that", "let's", "I'll go ahead and", "great question". Say the thing.
- Answer the exact question asked. No adjacent information, no background the user did not request, no options the user did not ask to compare.

tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file outside the working directory that you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

=== languages.py ===
"""Target query languages for the query-generation steps.

Each language records everything the generation steps need to differ on: the
prompt files, the output file extension, the comment prefix used when writing
headers or commenting out non-query blocks, and how a fenced code block in an
LLM response is recognised as a query.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Language:
    name: str
    query_prompt: str    # prompt for the per-smell step
    report_prompt: str   # prompt for the merged report step
    extension: str
    comment_prefix: str
    fence_tags: tuple[str, ...]   # fence tags that always mean "this is a query"
    query_re: re.Pattern[str]     # detects a query inside a bare ``` fence


GREMLIN = Language(
    name="gremlin",
    query_prompt="gen_query.txt",
    report_prompt="gen_report.txt",
    extension=".groovy",
    comment_prefix="//",
    fence_tags=("groovy", "gremlin"),
    query_re=re.compile(r"g\."),
)

SPARQL = Language(
    name="sparql",
    query_prompt="gen_sparql_query.txt",
    report_prompt="gen_sparql_report.txt",
    extension=".rq",
    comment_prefix="#",
    fence_tags=("sparql",),
    query_re=re.compile(r"(?:PREFIX|SELECT)", re.IGNORECASE),
)

"""Target query languages for the query-generation steps.

Each language records everything the generation steps need to differ on: the
prompt files, the output file extension, the comment prefix used when writing
headers or commenting out non-query blocks, and how a fenced code block in an
LLM response is recognised as a query.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Language:
    name: str
    query_prompt: str    # prompt for the per-smell step
    report_prompt: str   # prompt for the merged report step
    extension: str
    comment_prefix: str
    fence_tags: tuple[str, ...]   # fence tags that always mean "this is a query"
    query_re: re.Pattern[str]     # detects a query inside a bare ``` fence


GREMLIN = Language(
    name="gremlin",
    query_prompt="gen_query.txt",
    report_prompt="gen_report.txt",
    extension=".groovy",
    comment_prefix="//",
    fence_tags=("groovy", "gremlin"),
    query_re=re.compile(r"g\."),
)

SPARQL = Language(
    name="sparql",
    query_prompt="gen_sparql_query.txt",
    report_prompt="gen_sparql_report.txt",
    extension=".rq",
    comment_prefix="#",
    fence_tags=("sparql",),
    query_re=re.compile(r"(?:PREFIX|SELECT)", re.IGNORECASE),
)

content.text:
Branch `AI-1812-gremlin-sparql` in `ardoq-ai-research`. The changes add SPARQL as a second target language for the Query Generator, alongside Gremlin, by parameterising the existing generation steps instead of duplicating them.

**New: `ontology/src/pipeline/languages.py`**
A frozen `Language` dataclass holding everything the generation steps differ on: prompt filenames, output extension, comment prefix, fence tags, and a regex for detecting a query inside an untagged ``` block. Two instances: `GREMLIN` (`gen_query.txt`/`gen_report.txt`, `.groovy`, `//`, tags `groovy`/`gremlin`, matches `g.`) and `SPARQL` (`gen_sparql_query.txt`/`gen_sparql_report.txt`, `.rq`, `#`, tag `sparql`, matches `PREFIX`/`SELECT`).

**`llm_utils.py`** — de-hardcoded from Gremlin. `_is_gremlin` → `_is_query(fence_tag, content, lang)`; the `g.` regex is gone, replaced by `lang.query_re`. `_comment_out`, `extract_single_query`, and `extract_all_queries` now take a `lang` argument and use `lang.comment_prefix`.

**`gen_queries.py` / `gen_report.py`** — both `run()` functions take `lang: Language = GREMLIN` and use it to pick the prompt file, output extension, header comment prefix, and existing-output glob. Both CLIs gain `--lang {gremlin,sparql}`, which also selects the output directory.

**`config.py`** — four new output paths: `sparql_queries`, `sparql_extended`, `sparql_reports`, `sparql_report_extended` (under `data/sparql-*`), mirroring the existing Gremlin ones.

**`run_pipeline.py`** — four new steps: `queries-sparql`, `queries-sparql-ext`, `reports-sparql`, `reports-sparql-ext`, wired to the same `gen_queries.run`/`gen_report.run` with `lang=SPARQL`.

**New prompts: `gen_sparql_query.txt`, `gen_sparql_report.txt`**
Ports of the Gremlin prompts, but substantially longer because they encode GraphLake's RDF representation: the prefix set (`ardoq:`, `ardoq-common:`, etc.); graph patterns for "is a component/reference", component type by label, custom field values (two triples, since field types are their own nodes), and incoming/outgoing typed references; a warning that `?entity` must be positively bound before `FILTER NOT EXISTS`; that ordinary traversal uses the reference-type IRI as predicate directly and only a reference's own properties need the RDF 1.2 triple term `rdf:reifies <<( ... )>>`; that `@storage`/built-in-field `@db` annotations are Gremlin storage keys with no RDF meaning while custom-field and type `@db` values remain the literals to match; and literal typing rules, since GraphLake does no datatype inference (numbers `xsd:decimal`, dateTimes at second precision without timezone, enumerations as plain strings — read the declared range rather than guessing). Output contracts match the Gremlin prompts: per-smell queries project `?id`/`?name`/`?value`; report queries project `?id`/`?name` plus one `BIND(EXISTS {...} AS ?flag)` column per flagged class, split into one query per component type.

No generated SPARQL output is checked in, and there are no tests in the diff.

content.text:
Two senses, both from `gen_report.py` / the report prompts:

**Files**: one per group DL file, written to the language's report dir — `query{N}.groovy` (Gremlin) or `query{N}.rq` (SPARQL). If the LLM returns multiple queries, they're split into `query{N}-a`, `query{N}-b`, … If no query block is recognised, the raw response goes to `query{N}_raw.txt`.

**Query result shape**: one row per entity matching at least one flagged class, projecting `?id`, `?name`, and one boolean column per flagged class (`BIND(EXISTS {...} AS ?flagName)` in SPARQL).

message.content: what is the difference between the function of gen sparql query and gen sparql report?

content.text:
`gen_sparql_query.txt` is the per-smell prompt: it is rendered once per Flagged class (`{flagged}`) and asks for a single query that returns the entities violating that one class, projecting `?id`, `?name`, `?value`.

`gen_sparql_report.txt` is the per-group prompt: it is rendered once per group DL file with the whole list of Flagged classes (`{flagged_list}`) and asks for one query covering all of them at once, projecting `?id`, `?name` plus a boolean `BIND(EXISTS {...} AS ?flagName)` column per class — with an instruction to emit a separate query per component type if the classes span several.

So: one query per smell versus one merged multi-flag query per group. The rest of both prompts (prefixes, graph patterns, literal typing, `@storage`/`@db` rules) is identical.

message.content: in other words this has nothing to do with the actual ontology reports described in the documentation?

content.text:
Correct in that `gen_report.py` is a query-generation step, not the Report Generator component: it emits `.rq`/`.groovy` files and never executes anything or touches the report APIs. Its output is the merged multi-flag query variant, sitting in the Query Generator box.

Whether it is meant to feed the Report Generator is not stated anywhere in these files — the name and the row-per-entity/column-per-flag shape are table-shaped, but nothing in the diff references ardoq-api's report wrapper.

message.content: some of this language is gobbledygook to me. explain what the implications of each of the real problems are, concisely and simply

content.text:
Background needed for the first three: in RDF every value carries a datatype tag, and a query matches a value only if *both* the text and the tag are identical. `"3"^^xsd:integer` and `"3"^^xsd:decimal` are different terms. A tag mismatch is not an error — the query just matches nothing and returns an empty result. That's why these are dangerous: they look like "no problems found in the data" rather than a bug.

**1. Numbers are always tagged `xsd:decimal` in the real data.** The prompt tells the model to pick the tag from what the ontology declares the field to be, so for `maturity` (declared an integer) it will write `xsd:integer`. That matches nothing. Every smell about a numeric field silently reports zero results. This is the one that actually breaks output today.

**2. "GraphLake does no datatype inference" is not what happens.** There's a setting (entailment) under which the store ignores the tag and compares the text only. So the same query can behave differently depending on store configuration. The prompt states one absolute rule, so the model can't reason about the other case.

**3. Data loaded by different routes carries different, sometimes broken tags.** CSV import, the Cypher writer, the Gremlin writer and one REST endpoint each write numbers differently — one writes a malformed tag, another writes no tag at all. Consequence: a query can be correct by the prompt's rules and by the ontology, and still return nothing, purely because of how that customer's data got into the store. Correct query generation alone cannot guarantee correct results.

**4. The date format rule is unsupported guesswork.** The prompt asserts dates look like `"2026-03-15T11:45:30"` with second precision and no timezone. Nobody could find evidence for that — no production query uses dates at all. If the assertion is wrong, every date-based smell returns zero rows, same silent failure as (1). Currently unknown; checking how ardoq-api writes a date field would settle it.

**5. No rule for true/false fields.** The prompt covers numbers, dates and strings only. Real data writes booleans bare (`true`), but the model has no instruction, so it will guess — likely `"true"^^xsd:boolean` or `"true"` — and a wrong guess is another silent empty result. `approved` is such a field in the ontology.

**6. The "this thing is a component" line is optional in the prompt but universal in practice.** All ~200 hand-written production queries include it; this generation left it out. Low risk of wrong results, but it departs from the house pattern, and the agent noted it may affect which internal engine the query runs on.

**7. `?value` is required in the output but never defined.** The prompt says every query must return an `?id`, `?name` and `?value` column without saying what `?value` is. The model filled it with the name of the smell class — the same constant on every row, so the column is useless. It needs a definition (presumably the field value that triggered the flag) and a rule for smells that are purely structural, like "has no owner", where there is no such value.

lastPrompt: what is entailment mode? concise

content.text:
Entailment is the RDF store inferring facts that aren't literally stored but follow from the ontology — e.g. if `Application ⊑ Component` and X is an Application, a query for Components returns X even though no triple says so. It's a mode because the inference costs work, so it's switched on or off.

The specific quirk here is narrower than that general definition: per the agent's citation (`LITERAL_FINDINGS.md` #4, `query.go:8626`), when GraphLake runs with entailment on, a literal bound in a query is matched on its text alone and the datatype tag is ignored. So the same query can match or not match depending on the mode. I haven't verified that in the source myself.

lastPrompt: Explain concisely each of the steps that the pipeline goes through when you run the test we ran earlier. i.e., what ontology data is obtained, what is fed to claude and what other steps are involved

content.text:
For `python -m src.pipeline.gen_queries --lang sparql --test-run`:

1. **Resolve config** — `config.py` loads `ontology/.env` for `API_KEY`; `--lang sparql` selects the `SPARQL` Language (prompt files, `.rq`, `#`) and, with `--source inferred`, the output dir `data/sparql-queries/`, which is created if missing.
2. **Find inputs** — glob `data/dl-inferred/group*.dle`, sorted; six files exist, `group1.dle` is first.
3. **Load the shared context once** — `data/dl/foundation-core.dle` (542 lines: the full DLe ontology — classes, fields, reference types, their `@db`/`@label`/`@storage` annotations) and the prompt template `prompts/gen_sparql_query.txt`.
4. **Skip check** — if `data/sparql-queries/queries1.rq` already exists and `--force` wasn't passed, the group is skipped entirely. (This is why a re-run currently does nothing.)
5. **Extract the smells** — regex `^([a-zA-Z]+) ⊑ Flagged` over `group1.dle` finds seven Flagged classes, the first being `FlaggedUnownedApplication`.
6. **One API call per class** — for `FlaggedUnownedApplication`, a single user message with three text blocks: the whole of `foundation-core.dle`, the whole of `group1.dle` (36 lines, containing the DL definition of each Flagged class), and the prompt template with `{flagged}` substituted. Sent to `claude-sonnet-4-6` (`Models.query_gen`) via the streaming API, 16k max tokens, extended thinking enabled with a 15,999-token budget. No tools, no ontology API call, no store access — everything Claude sees is those two files plus the prompt.
7. **Post-process the response** — take the first text block; `extract_single_query` finds all fenced code blocks, keeps the *last* one recognised as SPARQL (by a ```` ```sparql ```` tag, or `PREFIX`/`SELECT` inside a bare fence) so self-corrections are discarded, and rewrites any non-query blocks as `#` comments.
8. **Write** — append a `# FlaggedUnownedApplication  (group1.dle)` header then the query to `data/sparql-queries/queries1.rq`, flush.
9. **Stop** — `--test-run` returns immediately after the first class, so the remaining six classes in `group1.dle` and all of `group2-6.dle` are never processed.

Explain each line of this sparql query: SELECT DISTINCT ?id ?name ?value
WHERE {
  # Required anchor
  ?entity rdf:type/rdfs:subClassOf/rdfs:subClassOf ardoq:Component .

  # Application type
  ?entity rdf:type/rdfs:label "Application" .

  # Bind identity fields before negation
  ?entity ardoq-common:id   ?id .
  ?entity ardoq-common:name ?name .

  # ∃consumedBy.⊤ — at least one incoming "Consumes" reference
  ?consumesType rdfs:label "Consumes" .
  ?consumesType rdfs:subClassOf/rdfs:subClassOf ardoq:Reference .
  ?consumer ?consumesType ?entity .

  # ¬∃realizes.⊤ — no "Is Realized By" reference points to this application
  # realizes ≡ isRealizedBy⁻, so ∃realizes.⊤ ↔ ∃ capability with isRealizedBy → entity
  FILTER NOT EXISTS {
    ?realizedByType rdfs:label "Is Realized By" .
    ?realizedByType rdfs:subClassOf/rdfs:subClassOf ardoq:Reference .
    ?capability ?realizedByType ?entity .
  }

  BIND("FlaggedConsumedButNoCapabilities" AS ?value)
}

content.text:
`SELECT DISTINCT ?id ?name ?value` — return three columns. `DISTINCT` matters here: the `Consumes` pattern below matches once per consumer, so an application consumed by five things would otherwise appear five times.

`?entity rdf:type/rdfs:subClassOf/rdfs:subClassOf ardoq:Component .` — the mandatory anchor. `/` is a property path: follow `rdf:type` from `?entity`, then `rdfs:subClassOf` twice, and require you land on `ardoq:Component`. Restricts `?entity` to component instances. The two subclass steps are the fixed depth of Ardoq's hierarchy (instance → its component type → … → `ardoq:Component`).

`?entity rdf:type/rdfs:label "Application" .` — follow `rdf:type` to the entity's component-type node, then its `rdfs:label`, and require the literal `"Application"`. Narrows to applications specifically. Component types are matched by their human-readable label, not by IRI.

`?entity ardoq-common:id ?id .` / `?entity ardoq-common:name ?name .` — read the built-in id and name into the projected variables. These also serve as the positive binding of `?entity` that must precede the negation below, so the `FILTER NOT EXISTS` is evaluated per candidate entity rather than over the whole graph. Side effect: because these are ordinary joins, an application with no `name` triple is dropped.

`?consumesType rdfs:label "Consumes" .` — find the reference-type node whose label is `"Consumes"`.

`?consumesType rdfs:subClassOf/rdfs:subClassOf ardoq:Reference .` — confirm that node really is a reference type, guarding against some other node happening to carry the same label.

`?consumer ?consumesType ?entity .` — the reference type node is used *as the predicate*: any `?consumer` linked to `?entity` by it. Because `?entity` is in the object position, this is the incoming direction — something consumes this application. At least one match is required, which is the `∃consumedBy.⊤` half of the smell.

`FILTER NOT EXISTS { … }` — keep only entities for which the enclosed pattern has no solution. Inside it, the same three-step idiom: locate the reference type labelled `"Is Realized By"`, verify it is a reference type, then look for any `?capability` pointing at `?entity` through it. So: discard any application that some capability does realize. `?capability` and `?realizedByType` exist only inside the braces.

`BIND("FlaggedConsumedButNoCapabilities" AS ?value)` — set `?value` to that fixed string on every row. It satisfies the prompt's three-column contract but carries no per-entity information; this is the `?value`-undefined prompt gap from the earlier review.

Not in the snippet: the query needs `PREFIX` declarations for `rdf:`, `rdfs:`, `ardoq:`, and `ardoq-common:` — as pasted it won't parse.

Net meaning: applications that something consumes, but which no capability is recorded as realizing.

def extract_dl_groups(text: str) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    """Parse an LLM response into (title, dl_content) pairs.

    Sections are delimited by '## Group N: Title' or '## Title' headers (two
    or three hashes). DL content is extracted from a ```dl fence if present,
    otherwise taken as raw text between headers.

    Returns an empty list if no headers are found.
    """
    headers = list(_DL_GROUP_HEADER_RE.finditer(text))
    if not headers:
        return []

    groups: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
    for i, header in enumerate(headers):
        title = header.group(1).strip()
        start = header.end()
        end = headers[i + 1].start() if i + 1 < len(headers) else len(text)
        section = text[start:end]

        dl_match = _DL_FENCE_RE.search(section)
        content = dl_match.group(1).strip() if dl_match else section.strip()

        if content:
            groups.append((title, content))

    return groups

content.text:
It's the shared plumbing between Claude and the pipeline steps — client construction plus response parsing. Nothing in it talks to the ontology or decides what to ask; it only builds the client and turns prose-with-code-fences into usable text.

Four public functions, used by the three generation steps:

- `create_client()` — builds the `anthropic.Anthropic` client from `API_KEY`. Used by all three steps.
- `extract_single_query(text, lang)` — for `gen_queries.py`. Finds all fenced blocks, keeps the **last** one recognised as a query in `lang` (so the model's self-corrections are discarded), and rewrites the non-query blocks as line comments so the prose survives in the output file.
- `extract_all_queries(text, lang)` — for `gen_report.py`. Returns **every** query block in order, since the report step legitimately produces one query per component type.
- `extract_dl_groups(text)` — for `infer_dl.py`, the upstream step. Splits a response into `(title, dl_content)` pairs on `## Group N: Title` headers, taking the content from a ```` ```dl ```` fence when present. This is what writes the `group*.dle` files the query steps later read.

Recognising a block as a query is `_is_query`: an explicit fence tag from `lang.fence_tags` always counts; a bare ``` fence is scanned for `lang.query_re` on its non-comment lines; any other tag is rejected. That function and `_comment_out` are where the Gremlin/SPARQL difference is consumed — they were the hardcoded `g.` regex and `//` prefix before the diff.

content.text:
Claude replies as one block of text. That text typically mixes explanation with code delimited by triple-backtick lines, e.g.:

````
Here's my first attempt:

```sparql
SELECT ?id WHERE { ... }
```

Actually that misses unnamed applications. Corrected:

```sparql
SELECT ?id ?name WHERE { ... }
```
````

The pipeline needs a `.rq` file containing just a query. `llm_utils.py` does that conversion. Concretely:

- `_CODE_BLOCK_RE` (line 11) matches each triple-backtick block, capturing the tag after the opening backticks (`sparql`, `groovy`, or nothing) and the body.
- `_is_query` (line 27) decides per block whether the body is a query: tag in `lang.fence_tags` → yes; empty tag → yes if any non-comment line matches `lang.query_re` (`PREFIX`/`SELECT` for SPARQL, `g.` for Gremlin); any other tag → no.
- `extract_single_query` (line 46) keeps the last such block — in the example above, the corrected query — and discards the earlier one. The explanation text between blocks is dropped; other fenced blocks are passed through `_comment_out`, which prefixes each of their lines with `#` so they stay in the file without breaking it.
- `extract_all_queries` (line 71) instead returns every query block, because `gen_report.py` asks for one query per component type and needs all of them.
- `extract_dl_groups` (line 84) is the same idea for the earlier `infer_dl.py` step: it splits the reply on `## Group 1: ...` headers and takes each section's ```` ```dl ```` block, producing the `(title, content)` pairs written out as `group1.dle` … `group6.dle`.
- `create_client` (line 16) reads `API_KEY` from the environment and returns the `anthropic.Anthropic` client the three steps call.

So: one place holding the API client plus the rules for finding the code inside Claude's replies. It sends nothing itself — `gen_queries.py` and `gen_report.py` own the API calls and pass the reply text in.

An N-Triples dump (1,241 triples, 202 KB, dated Sep 15) of the **Foundations metamodel as GraphLake stores it** — the metamodel only, no component or reference instances.

Contents by subject namespace:

| namespace | triples | what |
|---|---|---|
| `model/shapes/` | 420 | SHACL `NodeShape` (32) and `PropertyShape` (48) definitions — the per-field datatype constraints |
| `model/field-types/` | 250 | the 25 field definitions |
| `model/model-fields/` | 140 | which fields are attached to which model |
| `model/reference-types/` | 137 | the 15 reference types |
| `model/common/` | 111 | built-in predicates (`id`, `name`, `created`, …) |
| `meta-model/` | 68 | the `ardoq:` vocabulary itself |
| `model/component-types/` | 81 | 10 component types |
| `instances/workspaces/` | 28 | 4 workspaces: Organization, People, Applications, Business Capabilities |
| `instances/users/` | 6 | 2 users |

Component types: Application, Business Capability, Organization, Organizational Unit, Person. Reference types: Belongs To, Consumes, Has Successor, Is Expert In, Is Realized By, Owns, Reports To.

Fields (25), by `rdfs:label`: Application Ownership State, Application Type, Approved, Business Strategic Fit, Business Value, Complexity, Component Level, Contact Email, Criticality, Features and Usability, Functional Fit, Hosting Type, Lifecycle Phase, Live, Maintainability and Agility, Market Differentiation, Maturity, Organization URL, Ownership Accepted, Review Date, Service Level, Strategic Rating, Technical Fit, Technical Integrity, Technical Strategic Fit. Each carries `ardoq:name` (the lowercase query key, e.g. `maturity`), `ardoq:fieldType` (Ardoq's own kind: Number, List, …), `rdfs:comment`, and `rdfs:subClassOf`/`subPropertyOf ardoq:Field`.

Modelled as a hybrid: each field type is simultaneously an `owl:DatatypeProperty`, an `owl:Class`, and an `ardoq:CustomFieldType`. Field value datatypes are expressed as SHACL `sh:datatype` on a `PropertyShape` whose `sh:path` is the field type — 24 `xsd:string`, 6 `xsd:decimal`, 2 `xsd:dateTime`, 1 each of `xsd:boolean`, `xsd:date`, `xsd:anyURI`.

Directly relevant to the prompt work: this confirms the decimal rule from the store's own side. `maturity` and `complexity` both have `sh:datatype xsd:decimal` (shapes `a56f8762…`, `43a4ae81…`), as do `business_value`, `component_level`, `market_differentiation`, `technical_fit` — no numeric field is `xsd:integer`. `criticality` is `sh:datatype xsd:string` with `ardoq:fieldType "List"`, matching the prompt's string-enumeration claim. The only `xsd:integer` literals in the whole file are 28 `ardoq:order` values on metamodel elements, not field data.

The file also holds two `xsd:date`/`dateTime` fields (Review Date, plus one other) but no instance values, so it still does not settle the date literal format question — only the constraint, not what a written value looks like.

content.text:
Yes — several things, one of them material.

**1. Field types carry `ardoq:name`, not `ardoq-common:name`.** Both prompts instruct the two-triple field pattern as:

```
?fieldType ardoq-common:name "criticality" .
```

In this file every field type's query key is `<http://data.ardoq.com/meta-model/name>` (25 triples), and there are **zero** `model/common/name` triples on any field-type subject. Same split for ids: metamodel nodes use `ardoq:id`, instances use `ardoq-common:id`. This contradicts GraphLake's production query `026-...rq:14`, which uses `ardoq-common:name` on the field type. One of the two is wrong for any given store, and I can't tell which from this file alone — it depends on whether the live store is loaded by the same serializer that produced this dump. Worth resolving before the next generation run, since a wrong predicate here returns zero rows for every field-based smell.

**2. The SHACL shapes are the authoritative datatype source, and the prompts ignore them.** 48 `sh:PropertyShape` nodes give `sh:datatype` per field (`sh:path` → field type). That is exactly the information the prompts currently tell the model to derive from the DL declared range — the rule we just corrected by hand. The prompts declare the `sh:` prefix but never reference a shape. Feeding these shapes (or deriving the field-datatype table from them) would remove the guesswork instead of patching it.

**3. `ardoq:fieldType` states Ardoq's own field kind as a literal** — `"Number"` for maturity/complexity, `"List"` for criticality. A second, simpler signal for string-vs-number that the prompts don't mention.

**4. Component and reference types exist in two tiers, both labelled identically.** For "Application": a UUID node `a0a27382-…` with `rdfs:subClassOf ardoq:Component`, and a workspace-specific hex node `ebbf9b9c…` with `rdfs:subClassOf` that UUID node. Likewise "Owns": UUID `0c4a157e-…` at depth 1 and hex `36fb28f8…` at depth 2. This is why the anchor path has exactly two `rdfs:subClassOf` steps — the prompts state the depth as a bare fact without saying what the tiers are, so the model has no basis for adapting if a type sits at a different depth, and no warning that a bare `rdfs:label "Owns"` match binds two distinct nodes.

**5. Workspaces.** The file contains four workspace instances (Organization, People, Applications, Business Capabilities) typed `ardoq:Workspace`. Production bundle queries scope every query to a workspace id via `ardoq-common:workspace`. The prompts list that predicate among the built-ins but give no pattern and no instruction about whether generated queries should be workspace-scoped.

**6. `createdBy`/`lastModifiedBy` values are IRIs, not names.** They point to `instances/users/…` nodes typed `ardoq-common:User`, each carrying its own `ardoq-common:name` ("Graham Moore", "Tobias"). The prompts list the predicates without saying a second hop is needed to get a person's name — a smell like "applications last edited by X" would be written wrong.

**7. `ardoq-common:displayText` does not exist in this metamodel.** It's in both prompts' built-in list; zero occurrences in the file. Conversely the file defines `rootWorkspace`, `image`, `icon`, `color`, `shape` in the same namespace, and an `ardoq:Tag` class, none of which the prompts mention.

**8. Fields are `rdfs:subPropertyOf ardoq:Field`** (and types are `owl:Class` + `rdfs:Class`, field types additionally `owl:DatatypeProperty`). The subproperty link would allow "any field" queries; not mentioned in the prompts.

Minor: the only `xsd:integer` literals in the file are 28 `ardoq:order` values on metamodel elements, which corroborates that integers never appear as field data. `rdfs:comment` on each field and type carries the scale definitions (criticality 1-5 with meanings, maturity per TOGAF ACM) — largely duplicated in the `.dle` ontology the model already receives.

What this file still cannot settle: it holds no component or reference instances, so the `xsd:dateTime` format claim at `gen_sparql_query.txt:49` remains unverified — the shapes confirm two fields are date-typed, not what a written value looks like.

content.text:
Only one is a live defect: **#1, `ardoq:name` vs `ardoq-common:name` on field types.** If the dump reflects the store, every generated query that reads a custom field matches nothing, which is most of the smells. Nothing else in the list breaks a query that currently works.

Two matter conditionally, i.e. they break specific smells rather than all of them:
- **#5 workspace scoping** — without it queries run across all workspaces. Whether that's wrong depends on intent, but production queries all scope, so the generated ones are doing something different from the hand-written ones.
- **#6 `createdBy`/`lastModifiedBy` needing a second hop to a User node** — only bites a smell that filters on a person.

**#2 (SHACL shapes)** is not a defect now that the decimal and boolean rules are written into the prompts by hand. It matters as the better way to supply that information — it would make the typing rules derived rather than maintained.

The rest (#3, #4, #7, #8) are accuracy cleanups with no effect on results.

You wouldn't. Nothing in the smell descriptions supports it — `workspace` appears nowhere in any of the six `group*.dle` files.

The foundation ontology does carry workspace information, but not the kind a query needs. `foundation-core.dle:31-42` declares four workspace classes, and lines 45-67 give axioms like `Application ⊑ ∀rootWorkspace.ApplicationsWorkspace`. Those are class-level constraints; a SPARQL filter needs a workspace instance id (`ardoq-common:id "ceec9e14…"`, as in the production bundle queries), and no id appears in the ontology. The ids exist only in the `.nt` dump, which the generator never sees.

More to the point, for this metamodel scoping would be redundant: since every Application is constrained to the Applications workspace, `?entity rdf:type/rdfs:label "Application"` already confines results to that workspace. Scoping would only add anything if a customer had two workspaces holding the same component type — a situation the ontology, as written, rules out.

So I overstated #5 by calling it conditionally material. The production queries scope because each is generated for a specific workspace-scoped report, not because correctness demands it. There's also a naming mismatch worth noting if scoping ever is wanted: the ontology uses `rootWorkspace`, while both prompts list `ardoq-common:workspace` among the built-ins — the `.nt` file defines both.
